body_text:
A sentence $\varphi$ is *valid* (or a *tautology* in
propositional contexts), written $\models \varphi$, if it is
true in every conceivable interpretation. Conversely, $\varphi$
is *satisfiable* if there exists at least one interpretation in
which it is true.

A theory $\Gamma$ is satisfiable if its axioms possess a shared
model. Satisfiability is an inherently global property: every
finite subcollection of axioms may possess a model without the
entire theory being satisfiable, although in first-order logic
the celebrated Compactness Theorem guarantees that global
satisfiability is equivalent to finite satisfiability. The
construction of explicit models remains mathematics' principal
technique for proving that an assertion is independent of a
given set of axioms.
